rationale: A wins because it preserves a real buyer-ops lane that B throws in the trash. “Airbnb wants corporate travel managers to stop chasing employees for receipts” is a pitchable T&E/procurement trade story, while B’s refusal of “Travel managers finally get one dashboard for Airbnb” as “duplicate” wrongly collapses the customer protagonist into the channel-threat story. B is sharper in spots, especially “routing the expenses through Concur and Ramp,” but it leaves one usable press door unopened.
gaps_in_A: “Airbnb is building the exact infrastructure ... that hotel chains have used to lock in corporate travel budgets” overstates the supplied facts. Plausible, yes; proven, no.
“Story type: category-creation” is the wrong label for the 71% angle. The actual story is skeptical data scrutiny, not proof that Airbnb created a category.

“business-trends reporter or a features desk” is softer than the rest of A’s targeting. That angle needs a travel-industry data, corporate-travel policy, or business-of-travel reporter, not a vague features desk.
gaps_in_B: “Travel managers finally get one dashboard for Airbnb” as “duplicate” is the biggest miss. The buyer’s expense-reconciliation problem is structurally different from the hotels/TMC channel-threat story.
“Next step: journalist-fit-check” is premature. First pick the angle and build a small beat-specific list; fit-check comes after names exist.
“hotels, TMCs, and incumbent corporate-booking tools” crowds one angle with too many antagonists. A good pitch chooses the incumbent pressure point for the outlet.

“pushes Airbnb supply further toward professional operators” is an extrapolation from the badge requirements. It can be asked as a question, but it needs host adoption and verification proof before it becomes the claim.
